city.name: Philadelphia
summary: In 1776 Philadelphia was the largest city in the colonies, with about 30,000 people. William Penn had laid out a grid of straight streets two miles wide, from the Delaware to the Schuylkill, but the town filled only the blocks nearest the Delaware, from the wharves west to about Seventh Street. Brick houses, churches and markets lined the streets, and ships from Europe and the Caribbean crowded the wharves.

The Continental Congress met here, first at Carpenters' Hall in 1774, then at the State House, where it declared independence on 4 July 1776. A British army took the city in September 1777 and held it until June 1778, guarded by a line of redoubts to the north. Congress came back that summer.
city.note: Streets from OpenHistoricalMap (CC0). OpenHistoricalMap has no historic Delaware shore here, so the river is drawn by hand: everything east of Water Street today is later landfill, so the 1776 shore is pulled back to just east of Water Street. The wharves follow the pattern of period plans, not a survey. Houses between the streets are generated. Surviving buildings use their real outlines from OpenStreetMap; City Tavern and Graff House are modern copies on the original sites; the rest are placed from period plans. The British redoubts follow Lewis Nicola's survey of July 1778.

properties.name: Dock Creek
description: The tidal creek where Penn landed in 1682 and the town's first harbour. By 1776 it was a muddy, smelly inlet lined with tanneries and the Blue Anchor landing. It was arched over and filled in by 1784, and Dock Street now follows its curve.

properties.name: The Delaware wharves
description: Dozens of timber wharves ran out from Water Street along two miles of river front. Ships from London, the West Indies and every colonial port unloaded here, and Philadelphia's flour, bread and timber went out. It was the busiest port in British America.

properties.name: State House Yard
description: The open yard behind the State House, walled in 1770. On 8 July 1776 John Nixon read the Declaration of Independence aloud here to a crowd for the first time.

properties.name: Pennsylvania State House
description: The colony's assembly hall, finished in 1753 and now called Independence Hall. The Second Continental Congress met in its Assembly Room from 1775. It voted for independence on 2 July 1776 and adopted the Declaration two days later.
During the British occupation the building held American prisoners of war. Congress returned in July 1778.

properties.name: State House steeple
description: The brick tower on the south front, added in 1753, held the State House bell, later called the Liberty Bell. Its wooden steeple had rotted by the Revolution and was taken down in 1781.

properties.name: Carpenters' Hall
description: The guild hall of the Carpenters' Company, finished in 1774. The First Continental Congress met here in September and October 1774 to answer the Intolerable Acts.

properties.name: Library Company
description: America's first lending library, founded by Benjamin Franklin and friends in 1731. In 1776 its books filled the upstairs of Carpenters' Hall, and the delegates to Congress were allowed to borrow them.

properties.name: Library Hall
description: The Library Company's own building on Fifth Street, opened in 1791.

properties.name: City Tavern
description: Opened in 1773, the largest and finest tavern in the colonies. John Adams called it 'the most genteel tavern in America'. Delegates to both Congresses ate, drank and argued here, and the first Fourth of July dinner was held here in 1777. Today's building is a 1975 copy on the same site.

properties.name: London Coffee House
description: The merchants' meeting place at Front and Market Streets from 1754. Ships, cargoes and enslaved people were sold here, and news from the river arrived here first.

properties.name: Court House
description: The town hall and county court house of 1710, standing in the middle of High Street at Second Street. Speeches were made and proclamations read from its balcony.

properties.name: High Street Market
description: Long open sheds down the middle of High Street (now Market Street). Farmers from Pennsylvania and New Jersey sold meat, butter and vegetables here on Wednesdays and Saturdays.

properties.name: Great Meeting House
description: The main Quaker meeting house, at Second and Market Streets. Many Quakers refused to take sides in the war, and some were exiled to Virginia in 1777 as suspected Loyalists.

properties.name: Christ Church
description: The Anglican church of 1744. Its 196-foot steeple, finished in 1754, was the tallest structure in North America. Washington, Franklin and Betsy Ross worshipped here, and seven signers of the Declaration are buried in its graveyards.

properties.name: Christ Church Burial Ground
description: The church's second graveyard, opened in 1719 at Fifth and Arch Streets. Benjamin Franklin was buried here in 1790.

properties.name: Elfreth's Alley
description: A narrow lane of small brick houses for tradesmen, opened about 1703 between Front and Second Streets. Blacksmiths, shipwrights, pewterers and their families lived here. It is the oldest residential street in America still lived in.

properties.name: Graff House
description: A new brick house at Seventh and Market Streets, on the edge of town. Thomas Jefferson rented two rooms on the second floor and wrote the draft of the Declaration of Independence here in June 1776. The house standing today is a 1975 copy.

properties.name: Walnut Street Jail
description: The new city jail, built from 1773 to 1776 across from the State House Yard. In the British occupation it held American prisoners, hundreds of whom died of hunger and cold. Many were buried in the square opposite.

properties.name: Southeast Square (Potter's Field)
description: One of the five open squares of William Penn's plan, used as a burial ground for strangers and the poor. In 1776 and 1777 thousands of Continental soldiers and prisoners who died of wounds and camp fever were buried here in long trenches. It is now Washington Square.

properties.name: St. Peter's Church
description: An Anglican chapel of ease for Christ Church, opened in 1761 for the families of Society Hill. Its tower and spire came later, in 1842.

properties.name: Gloria Dei (Old Swedes')
description: The church of the Swedish settlers who farmed here before Penn came, built in 1700. It is the oldest church in Pennsylvania.

properties.name: British redoubts
description: After taking the city in September 1777, the British dug ten square earth forts across the fields north of town, from the Delaware to the Schuylkill, joined by a barrier of felled trees. About 50 men held each one. Washington's army, camped at Valley Forge that winter, never attacked them. The British marched out on 18 June 1778.
